facts.statement: Tylosaurus lived between 92 and 66 million years ago during the Turonian and Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus (; "knob lizard") is a genus of russellosaurine mosasaur (an extinct group of predatory marine lizards) that lived about 92 to 66 million years ago during the Turonian to Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: The largest species, T. rex, is estimated to have reached over 13 meters in length and weighed nearly 8.4 tonnes.
facts.quote: The genus contains at least ten validly named species, the largest of which, T. rex, estimated to have reached over 13 m long and weighed nearly 8.4 t.

facts.statement: Fossils of Tylosaurus have been found primarily around the North Atlantic Ocean, including in North America, Europe, and Africa.
facts.quote: Its fossils have been found primarily around North Atlantic Ocean including in North America, Europe, and Africa.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus possessed an endothermic metabolism, a trait unlike nearly all modern squamates.
facts.quote: It had an endothermic metabolism, which is unlike nearly all modern squamates.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope presented a preliminary description of the type specimen in 1869, initially naming it Macrosaurus proriger.
facts.quote: Cope borrowed the specimen from Agassiz and presented a preliminary description of it in 1869. His first publication of the fossil was very brief and was named Macrosaurus proriger

facts.statement: In 1872, Othniel Charles Marsh erected the genus Rhinosaurus, meaning "nose lizard," derived from Ancient Greek words for nose and lizard.
facts.quote: In 1872, Marsh argued that L. proriger is taxonomically distinct from the European genus and must be assigned a new one. For this, he erected the genus Rhinosaurus, which means "nose lizard" and is a portmanteau derived from the Ancient Greek words ῥίς (, meaning "nose") and σαῦρος (, meaning "lizard").

facts.statement: Marsh suggested the genus name Tylosaurus, meaning "knob lizard," derived from the Latin word for knob and the Ancient Greek word for lizard, referencing the animal's elongated snout.
facts.quote: As a result, he suggested a move to a newly erected genus named Tylosaurus. This name means "knob lizard" in another reference to the elongated rostrum characteristic of the genus. It is derived from the Latin tylos (knob) and Ancient Greek σαῦρος.

facts.statement: The species T. nepaeolicus was formally transferred to the genus Tylosaurus in 1894 by John Campbell Merriam.
facts.quote: This species, whose specific epithet refers to Nepaholla, the Native American name for the Salomon River is formally transferred to the genus Tylosaurus in 1894 by John Campbell Merriam.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope persisted in using the genus Liodon for T. nepaeolicus, a species whose type specimen was discovered by Benjamin Franklin Mudge near the Solomon River.
facts.quote: Cope's persistence can be seen in his 1874 description of another species which he named L. nepaeolicus. The type specimen of this species was discovered by Benjamin Franklin Mudge near the Solomon River, and consists of several cranial fragments and a dorsal vertebra now catalogued as AMNH 1565.

facts.statement: In 1804, the Lewis and Clark Expedition discovered a fossil skeleton along the Missouri River that was identified as a 45-foot-long fish.
facts.quote: In 1804, the Lewis and Clark Expedition discovered a now-lost fossil skeleton alongside the Missouri River, which was identified as a 45 ft long fish.

facts.statement: Louis Dollo described the species Hainosaurus bernardi in 1885 based on a skeleton found in a phosphate quarry in the Ciply Basin of Mesvin, Belgium.
facts.quote: In 1885, Louis Dollo described the genus and species Hainosaurus bernardi from an almost complete but poorly preserved skeleton discovered in a phosphate quarry in the Ciply Basin of Mesvin, Belgium, since numbered as IRSNB R23.

facts.statement: The name Hainosaurus refers to the Haine river near the fossil site in Belgium.
facts.quote: The genus name Hainosaurus means "lizard from the Haine", in reference to the eponymous river located nearby the Ciply Basin.

facts.statement: Elizabeth Nicholls described a second species formerly in Hainosaurus in 1988 from a partial skeleton found in Manitoba, Canada.
facts.quote: In 1988, a second species historically pertained to Hainosaurus was described by Elizabeth Nicholls based on a partial skeleton catalogued as MT 2 and having been discovered in Manitoba, Canada.

facts.statement: Timon Bullard and Michael Caldwell moved the species to the genus Tylosaurus in 2010 and renamed it T. pembinensis.
facts.quote: it was in a revision published in 2010 that the species was moved to Tylosaurus by Timon Bullard and Michael Caldwell, being then renamed as T. pembinensis.

facts.statement: Paulina Jimenez-Huidobro and Michael Caldwell transferred Hainosaurus bernardi to Tylosaurus in 2016, renaming it T. bernardi.
facts.quote: This redescription was finally carried out by Paulina Jimenez-Huidobro and Caldwell in 2016, in which they transferred the species to Tylosaurus, being then renamed as T. bernardi.

facts.statement: Some researchers argue that the genus Hainosaurus should remain distinct from Tylosaurus based on dental traits.
facts.quote: Although this new combination has been widely recognized since, some authors nevertheless suggest continuing to maintain the genus Hainosaurus as distinct, justified in particular on the basis of dental traits not detailed in the 2016 revision.

facts.statement: Armand Thevenin described a new mosasaurid in 1896 from a partial skull found at Éclusier-Vaux in Somme, France.
facts.quote: In 1896, Armand Thevenin described a new mosasaurid on the basis of a partial skull discovered at Éclusier-Vaux, in Somme, France.

facts.statement: Johan Lindgren reassigned the species to Tylosaurus in 2005 because its dental characteristics matched other members of the genus.
facts.quote: In 2005, Lindgren moved this species to Tylosaurus, notably due to its dental characteristics being closer to other members of the genus.

facts.statement: Per Ove Persson identified a new mosasaurid in 1963 from isolated teeth found in Ivö Klack, Sweden.
facts.quote: In 1963, Per Ove Persson identified a new mosasaurid on the basis of isolated teeth discovered in a deposit located in Ivö Klack, near Ivö Lake in the Kristianstad Basin in Scania, Sweden.

facts.statement: Lindgren and Mikael Siverson reassigned the taxon to Tylosaurus in 2002 and included additional fossils from Ivö Klack, such as cranial and vertebral remains.
facts.quote: When the taxon was significantly revised in a in 2002 study, being reassigned to Tylosaurus, Lindgren and Mikael Siverson referred additional fossils to this latter that had been discovered at Ivö Klack, including cranial and vertebral remains.

facts.statement: A 2008 discovery of Taniwhasaurus in Japan revived the hypothesis that T. ivoensis might belong to that genus, though this remains a subject for future study.
facts.quote: However, in 2008, Caldwell and colleagues reported the presence of Taniwhasaurus in northern Japan and reaffirmed the dental similarities with T. ivoensis. This discovery revived the hypothesis of a possible reassignment of the species to Taniwhasaurus, but the authors see this as a subject for another study.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope described the holotype of T. proriger in 1870 and visualized it as an excessively elongated reptile.
facts.quote: When Cope described the holotype specimen of T. proriger in 1870, he visualized it as an "excessively elongated reptile", due the morphological arrangement of its caudal vertebrae.

facts.statement: Cope described the head of Tylosaurus as conical with eyes on top and a pelican-like throat to help swallow prey.
facts.quote: For him, the head of Tylosaurus would be conical in shape, with eyes on top, and having a jaw connected to a throat similar to that of a pelican, thus facilitating the entry of its prey.

facts.statement: Cope believed Tylosaurus had only front flippers and lacked rear flippers.
facts.quote: Still according to Cope, the animal would have had only the flippers located at the front of the body, those at the back being absent.

facts.statement: Cope depicted Tylosaurus as having a long, flat tail used for eel-like swimming.
facts.quote: The tail is seen as long and flat, used in eel-like locomotion.

facts.statement: Samuel Wendell Williston began the modern understanding of Tylosaurus anatomy in 1898 with a major revision of Kansas mosasaurs.
facts.quote: Modern understanding of the anatomy of Tylosaurus started as early as 1898 with the publication of a major revision of the Kansas mosasaurs by Samuel Wendell Williston.

facts.statement: Williston estimated the maximum length of Tylosaurus at approximately 11 meters, a figure close to modern estimates.
facts.quote: Williston also estimated the maximum length of the animal at approximately 11 m, a value close to those still proposed today.

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn revealed the first substantially complete skeleton of Tylosaurus in 1899.
facts.quote: The discovery of the first known substantially complete skeleton of Tylosaurus was revealed as early as 1899 by Henry Fairfield Osborn, followed by other more or less similar finds which were made from the beginning of the 1900s.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus was a derived mosasaur with advanced traits including a fully aquatic lifestyle.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus was a type of derived mosasaur, or a latecoming member with advanced evolutionary traits such as a fully aquatic lifestyle.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus had a streamlined body, an elongated tail with a downturned two-lobed fin, and two pairs of flippers.
facts.quote: As such, it had a streamlined body, an elongated tail ending with a downturn supporting a two-lobed fin, and two pairs of flippers.

facts.statement: Modern understanding shows derived mosasaurs like Tylosaurus were built like ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and whales rather than sea snakes.
facts.quote: While in the past derived mosasaurs were depicted as akin to giant flippered sea snakes, it is now understood that they were more similar in build to other large marine vertebrates such as ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and archaeocete whales through convergent evolution.

facts.statement: The largest well-known Tylosaurus specimen is nicknamed "Bunker" and is housed at the University of Kansas Natural History Museum.
facts.quote: The largest well-known specimen is a skeleton of T. rex from the University of Kansas Natural History Museum nicknamed "Bunker" (KUVP 5033).

facts.statement: In 2026, researchers estimated the largest Tylosaurus specimen was 13.2 meters long, while the species generally ranged from 7.7 to 13.2 meters.
facts.quote: In 2026, Zietlow and colleagues estimated its size around 13.2 m, with the species as a whole ranging between 7.7-13.2 m.

facts.statement: A mounted skeleton of T. pembinensis nicknamed "Bruce" measures 13.05 meters long and held the Guinness World Record for "Largest mosasaur on display" in 2014.
facts.quote: A mounted skeleton of T. pembinensis, nicknamed "Bruce," at the Canadian Fossil Discovery Centre measures at 13.05 m long and was awarded a Guinness World Records for "Largest mosasaur on display" in 2014.

facts.statement: The genus Tylosaurus exhibits Cope's rule, showing a general increase in body size over geologic time.
facts.quote: The genus exhibits Cope's rule, in which its body size has been observed to generally increase over geologic time.

facts.statement: Everhart speculated that extremely old Tylosaurus individuals could have reached a maximum length of 20 meters due to continuous growth, though fossil evidence for such sizes is lacking.
facts.quote: Everhart speculated that because mosasaurs continuously grew throughout their lifetime, it would have been possible for some extremely old Tylosaurus individuals to reach 20 m in absolute maximum length.

facts.statement: The largest known Tylosaurus skull belongs to the "Bunker" specimen and is estimated to be up to 1.63 meters long.
facts.quote: The largest known skull of Tylosaurus is T. rex KUVP 5033 (the "Bunker" specimen), estimated up to 1.63 m long.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus skulls ranged from 13% to 14% of the total skeleton length depending on age and individual variation.
facts.quote: Depending on age and individual variation, Tylosaurus skulls were between 13 and 14% of the total skeleton length.

facts.statement: The Tylosaurus head was strongly conical with a snout proportionally longer than most mosasaurs, except Ectenosaurus.
facts.quote: The head was strongly conical and the snout proportionally longer than most mosasaurs, with the exception of Ectenosaurus.

facts.statement: The frontal bone in Tylosaurus usually has a low midline crest, most prominent in T. proriger and moderately developed in T. saskatchewanensis and T. bernardi.
facts.quote: The frontal bone in Tylosaurus usually, but not always, possesses a low midline crest. It is most prominent in T. proriger, and is moderately developed in T. saskatchewanensis and T. bernardi, extending onto the premaxilla in the latter.

facts.statement: The jugal bone forms the bottom of the orbit in Tylosaurus, is L-shaped, and has a distinctive extension called the posteroventral process.
facts.quote: The jugal forms the bottom of the orbit; in Tylosaurus, it is L-shaped and has a distinctive serif-like extension at the lower back corner of the junction between the horizontal and vertical rami (arms) called the posteroventral process.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus is one of the few mosasaurs with clearly documented nasal bones, the other being the holotype of Plotosaurus (though one bone is missing there).
facts.quote: Tylosaurus is one of the only mosasaurs in which the nasal bones are clearly documented; the other is the holotype of Plotosaurus, although one of the bones is missing.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus possessed 2 premaxillary, 12 to 13 maxillary, 13 dentary, and 10 to 11 pterygoid teeth on each side of its skull.
facts.quote: On each side of the skull, Tylosaurus had 2 premaxillary teeth, 12 to 13 maxillary teeth, 13 dentary teeth, and 10 to 11 pterygoid teeth.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus had homodont dentition where all teeth were nearly identical in size and shape except for the smaller, more recurved pterygoid teeth.
facts.quote: The dentition is homodont, meaning that all teeth are nearly identical in size and shape, with the exception of the pterygoid teeth, which are smaller and more recurved than the marginal teeth.

facts.statement: Carinae in T. rex and sometimes T. proriger were finely serrated with small denticles, whereas those in T. nepaeolicus and T. kansasensis were smooth.
facts.quote: Carinae (cutting edges) are finely serrated with small denticles in T. rex and sometimes T. proriger, which appear similar to those in Prognathodon and Mosasaurus though not as developed as in theropod dinosaurs or living monitors, and smooth in T. nepaeolicus and T. kansasensis.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the ivoensis group of Tylosaurus species constitutes a valid distinct classification.
facts.quote: The distinction of an ivoensis group is contentious.

facts.statement: The enamel surface of Tylosaurus teeth was lined with thin fine ridges called striations running vertically from the base.
facts.quote: The enamel surface is lined with thin fine ridges called striations that run vertically from the tooth's base.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus tooth surfaces were either smooth or faintly faceted, forming a prism-like geometry with multiple flat sides.
facts.quote: The surface is also either smooth or faintly faceted, in which it is flattened into multiple sides to form a prism-like geometry.

facts.statement: Adult Tylosaurus had unfused pectoral and pelvic girdles, unlike other taxa such as Prognathodon overtoni.
facts.quote: Both pectoral and pelvic girdles are unfused in adult Tylosaurus, in contrast to other taxa (e.g., Prognathodon overtoni).

facts.statement: Tylosaurus is distinguished from other mosasaurs by a scapula significantly smaller than the coracoid, the absence of anterior coracoid emargination, and the lack of a well-developed pubic tubercle.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus is also distinguished from other mosasaurs by a scapula that is significantly smaller than the coracoid and the absence of the anterior emargination of the coracoid, as well as the absence of a well-developed pubic tubercle.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus exhibited hyperphalangy with spindle-shaped phalanges in both fore- and hindlimbs, contrasting with the short, blocky hourglass-shaped phalanges of mosasaurines.
facts.quote: Hyperphalangy (increased number of phalanges relative to the ancestral condition) is present in both fore- and hindlimbs, and the phalanges are spindle-shaped, unlike the short, blocky hourglass-shaped phalanges possessed by mosasaurines.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus skin scales were small, diamond-shaped, and arranged in oblique rows similar to those of modern rattlesnakes.
facts.quote: These scales were small and diamond-shaped and were arranged in oblique rows, comparable to that found in modern rattlesnakes and other related reptiles.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus scales were keeled in a form resembling shark denticles.
facts.quote: Each scale was keeled in a form resembling that of a shark's denticles.

facts.statement: A 5-meter-long Tylosaurus had dermal scales measuring 3.3 mm, with an average of ninety scales per square inch on its underside.
facts.quote: An individual measuring 5 m in total body length had dermal scales measuring 3.3 x, and in each square inch (2.54 cm) of the mosasaur's underside an average of ninety scales were present.

facts.statement: Dark coloration in Tylosaurus likely helped maintain elevated body temperatures in colder environments by increasing heat absorption.
facts.quote: Dark coloration increases absorption of heat, allowing the animal to maintain elevated body temperatures in colder environments.

facts.statement: The paired bronchi in Tylosaurus suggest it had two functional lungs, similar to modern limbed lizards but unlike snakes.
facts.quote: The pairing is suggestive of two functional lungs like modern limbed lizards but unlike snakes.

facts.statement: In the Tylosaurus specimen, the point where the bronchi split occurs between the first and sixth cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: The bifurcation point for the Tylosaurus specimen is anywhere between the first and sixth cervical vertebrae.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus is classified in the family Mosasauridae within the superfamily Mosasauroidea.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus is classified within the family Mosasauridae in the superfamily Mosasauroidea.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus is the type genus of the subfamily Tylosaurinae.
facts.quote: The genus is the type genus of its own subfamily, the Tylosaurinae.

facts.statement: The subfamily Tylosaurinae is defined by an elongated premaxillary rostrum that lacks teeth.
facts.quote: The subfamily is defined by a shared feature of an elongated premaxillary rostrum that does not bear teeth.

facts.statement: The oldest known fossil of Tylosaurus is a premaxilla from the Arcadia Park Shale in Texas, dated between 92.1 and 91.4 million years ago.
facts.quote: The oldest fossil attributable to the genus is a premaxilla (TMM 40092-27) recovered from Middle Turonian deposits of the Arcadia Park Shale in Texas, which is dated between 92.1 and 91.4 million years old based on correlations with index fossils.

facts.statement: A skull from the Ojinaga Formation in Chihuahua, Mexico, attributed to an indeterminate Tylosaurus species, dates to at least 90 million years ago.
facts.quote: A slightly younger specimen is of a skull (SGM-M1) of an indeterminate Tylosaurus species similar to T. kansasensis from the Ojinaga Formation in Chihuahua, Mexico, dated around ~90 million years old at earliest.

facts.statement: When Hainosaurus is treated as a synonym, Tylosaurus represents one of the last surviving mosasaur genera.
facts.quote: With the incorporation of Hainosaurus as a synonym of Tylosaurus, this also makes the genus one of the last mosasaurs.

facts.statement: Scientists currently recognize nine valid species of Tylosaurus.
facts.quote: Currently, nine species of Tylosaurus are recognized by scientists as taxonomically valid.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Tylosaurus kansasensis is synonymous with T. nepaeolicus, and the taxon T. borealis has not yet been formally described.
facts.quote: There is still debate whether T. kansasensis is synonymous with T. nepaeolicus, and T. "borealis" has yet to be described in a formal publication.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Tylosaurus may have rapidly filled an ecological niche left by the extinction of pliosaurs and the decline of polycotylids.
facts.quote: Madiza and Cau proposed that Tylosaurus may have taken advantage of the extinction of the pliosaurs and decline of polycotylids to quickly fill the ecological void they left behind.

facts.statement: An alternative hypothesis suggests T. proriger evolved through peramorphosis, developing adult traits during its immature stage.
facts.quote: Second, the same study proposed an alternative hypothesis of peramorphosis, in which T. proriger evolved by developing traits found in mature T. nepaeolicus during immaturity.

facts.statement: Current phylogenetic analyses suggesting a paraphyletic Tylosaurus are considered preliminary, and future studies may yield different results.
facts.quote: However, the authors note that this represents a preliminary result of a work in progress matrix, and that future analyses with the inclusion of additional characters and taxa may lead to different results.

facts.statement: Russell (1967) proposed that Tylosaurus used its elongated rostrum to stun prey or defend against sharks.
facts.quote: Russell (1967) first speculated the elongated rostrum was used to "stun" prey or defend against sharks, though provided no further explanation.

facts.statement: Lingham-Soliar suggested that Tylosaurus used its rostrum as a battering ram to ram opponents.
facts.quote: Lingham-Soliar reasoned that such biomechanical adaptations allowed Tylosaurus to use its rostrum as a battering ram.

facts.statement: Lingham-Soliar (1998) argued that a fractured braincase in a subadult Mosasaurus skull was caused by a ramming attack from a T. bernardi.
facts.quote: Lingham-Soliar (1998) would later suggest possible evidence of a ram-attack in action in the skull of a subadult Mosasaurus whose braincase was fractured in life by a concentrated force, which he argued was rammed by a T. bernardi due to lack of damage elsewhere in the skull that would indicate other causes of injury.

facts.statement: Lingham-Soliar doubted the rostrum was used for sexual selection because surveys found no evidence of sexual dimorphism in rostrum length.
facts.quote: Lingham-Soliar doubted that the elongated rostrum was involved in sexual selection, such as male-male combat, as previous surveys of Tylosaurus skulls found no evidence of sexual dimorphism in the length of the rostrum.

facts.statement: Konishi et al. (2018) found the rostrum grew early in development, suggesting it was for general use like ramming rather than sexual selection.
facts.quote: Konishi et al.'s (2018) finding that the edentulous rostrum began to grow exceptionally early in development, which should not occur if the trait was sexual in nature but reasonable for general-purpose use like ramming.

facts.statement: An alternate hypothesis suggests Tylosaurus used its rostrum as a sensory tool.
facts.quote: An alternate hypothesis holds that the rostrum was used as a sensory tool.

facts.statement: Álvarez–Herrera et al. (2020) found a large network of ophthalmic nerve canals with up to 16 branching terminals in the rostrum of a Taniwhasaurus skull.
facts.quote: Álvarez–Herrera et al. (2020) based on CT scans of a Taniwhasaurus skull. They discovered a large network of internal canals of the ophthalmic nerve along the rostrum with up to 16 branching terminals inside the front end of the premaxilla, half of which exit into external foramina that dot the front and dorsal surfaces of the bone's edentulous region.

facts.statement: The high concentration of sensory nerves in the rostrum suggests it housed a mechanosensory or electrosensory organ.
facts.quote: The high concentration of sensory nerves within the edentulous portion of the rostrum suggests that it housed a mechanosensory or electrosensory organ.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggested the nerve branching in the rostrum was associated with blood supply pathways for thermoregulation.
facts.quote: It was also suggested that the heavy branching inside the rostrum is associated with pathways for blood supply, and therefore a thermoregulation mechanism.

facts.statement: The youngest known Tylosaurus specimen is a newborn estimated to be 30 cm in skull length and 2.23 meters in total length.
facts.quote: The youngest known Tylosaurus individual (FHSM VP-14845) is a newborn (neonate) estimated to have measured 30 cm in skull length and 2.23 m in total length

facts.statement: Juvenile Tylosaurus showed rapid growth in the first few years before slowing to a steady rate starting around year 5 or 6.
facts.quote: Both showed similar logarithmic growth curves that grew rapidly in the first few years but reduced to a steadier rate starting year 5 in the older specimen and year 6 in the younger

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Tylosaurus was larger at birth compared to other mosasaur genera like Platecarpus and Clidastes.
facts.quote: The distance of first-year LAGs to the bone center in both specimens were longer than those in Platecarpus and Clidastes humeri, which suggests that Tylosaurus was larger at birth

facts.statement: Tylosaurus had an accelerated growth rate similar to modern monitor lizards, likely due to the need for higher metabolic rates in an aquatic environment.
facts.quote: Like the other two mosasaurs, the overall growth rate was similar to modern monitor lizards but accelerated, which Pellegrini attributed to the need for increased metabolic rates to adapt to an aquatic environment

facts.statement: Research suggests that some traits previously interpreted as growth stages in T. proriger and T. nepaeolicus are actually variations between different species.
facts.quote: Zietlow also found that several traits she previously interpreted as part of growth stages in T. proriger and T. nepaeolicus in her 2020 study were actually interspecific variation

facts.statement: New analysis suggests T. kansasensis was not an immature form of T. nepaeolicus but a distinct species.
facts.quote: Zietlow also found that several traits she previously interpreted as part of growth stages in T. proriger and T. nepaeolicus in her 2020 study were actually interspecific variation, suggesting that T. kansasensis was not an immature form of T. nepaeolicus

facts.statement: Unlike most squamates, mosasaurs like Tylosaurus were likely endothermic, or warm-blooded.
facts.quote: Nearly all squamates are characterized by their cold-blooded ectothermic metabolism, but mosasaurs like Tylosaurus are unique in that they were likely endothermic, or warm-blooded

facts.statement: Analysis of eleven Tylosaurus specimens calculated an average internal body temperature of 34.3 degrees Celsius.
facts.quote: Analyzing the isotope levels of eleven Tylosaurus specimens an average internal body temperature of 34.3 C was calculated

facts.statement: Studies calculated body temperatures for Platecarpus and Clidastes at 36.3 C and 33.1 C respectively, similar to Tylosaurus.
facts.quote: Harrell, Pérez‐Huerta, and Suarez also calculated the body temperatures of Platecarpus and Clidastes with similar numbers, 36.3 C and 33.1 C respectively

facts.statement: The similar body temperatures of smaller mosasaurs suggest Tylosaurus's temperature was not due to gigantothermy but likely endothermy.
facts.quote: The fact that the other mosasaurs were much smaller in size than Tylosaurus and yet maintained similar body temperatures made it unlikely that Tylosauruss body temperature was the result of another metabolic type like gigantothermy

facts.statement: Endothermy likely provided Tylosaurus with advantages such as increased stamina, access to colder waters, and adaptation to Late Cretaceous cooling.
facts.quote: Endothermy would have provided several advantages to Tylosaurus such as increased stamina for foraging larger areas and pursuing prey, the ability to access colder waters, and better adaptation to withstand the gradual cooling of global temperatures during the Late Cretaceous

facts.statement: Bite marks suggest Tylosaurus also preyed on giant squid and ammonites.
facts.quote: Additional evidence from bite marks suggests the animal also preyed on giant squid and ammonites.

facts.statement: A 1987 find revealed a T. proriger skeleton containing the stomach contents of a 2-meter-long mosasaur, a diving bird, a fish, and possibly a shark.
facts.quote: The enormous and varied appetite of Tylosaurus can be demonstrated in a 1987 find that identified fossils of a mosasaur measuring 2 m or longer, the diving bird Hesperornis, a Bananogmius fish, and possibly a shark all within the stomach of a single T. proriger skeleton (SDSM 10439) recovered from the Pierre Shale of South Dakota.

facts.statement: Puncture marks on ammonites, the carapace of Protostega, and the gladius of Enchoteuthis have been attributed to Tylosaurus.
facts.quote: Puncture marks on fossils of ammonites, the carapace of a Protostega, and the gladius of an Enchoteuthis have been attributed to Tylosaurus.

facts.statement: Fossils with injuries inflicted by their own kind suggest Tylosaurus behavior towards each other was mostly aggressive.
facts.quote: The behavior of Tylosaurus towards each other may have been mostly aggressive, evidenced by fossils with injuries inflicted by another of their own kind.

facts.statement: A 5-meter-long T. kansasensis holotype shows injuries indicating it was killed by a larger Tylosaurus in a fatal intraspecific combat.
facts.quote: At least one fatal instance of intraspecific combat among Tylosaurus is documented in the holotype of the discussed species T. kansasensis (FHSM VP-2295), representing a 5 m long animal, which possesses numerous injuries that indicate it was killed by a larger Tylosaurus.

facts.statement: The skull roof and dentary of a T. kansasensis specimen exhibit four massive gouges and at least seven puncture wounds and gouges.
facts.quote: The skull roof and surrounding areas exhibit signs of trauma in the form of four massive gouges, and the dentary contains at least seven puncture wounds and gouges.

facts.statement: Between 3-15% of vertebrae in North American Tylosaurus and 16% in T. bernardi were affected by avascular necrosis.
facts.quote: The study observed that between 3-15% of vertebrae in the spinal column of North American Tylosaurus and 16% of vertebrae in T. bernardi were affected by avascular necrosis.

facts.statement: Carlsen (2017) posited that Tylosaurus lacked necessary adaptations for deep diving despite having well-developed eardrums, suggesting the cause of avascular necrosis is debated.
facts.quote: Carlsen (2017) posited that Tylosaurus gained avascular necrosis because it lacked the necessary adaptations for deep or repetitive diving, although noted that the genus had well-developed eardrums that could protect themselves from rapid changes in pressure.

facts.statement: Some Tylosaurus skeletons show unnatural fusion of tail vertebrae, sometimes forming a single mass called a "club tail."
facts.quote: Unnatural fusion of some vertebrae in the tail has been reported in some Tylosaurus skeletons. A variation of these fusions may concentrate near the end of the tail to form a single mass of multiple fused vertebrae called a "club tail."

facts.statement: Rothschild and Everhart (2015) found that five of 23 surveyed North American Tylosaurus skeletons exhibited fused tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: Rothschild and Everhart (2015) surveyed 23 North American Tylosaurus skeletons and one T. bernardi skeleton and found that five of the North American skeletons exhibited fused tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: A juvenile Tylosaurus with a club tail had a shark tooth embedded in the fusion, confirming some cases were caused by predator attacks.
facts.quote: One juvenile specimen with the club tail condition was found with a shark tooth embedded in the fusion, which confirms that at least some cases were caused by infections inflicted by predator attacks.

facts.statement: A T. kansasensis specimen has two fully healed fractured ribs, and a T. proriger skull shows a fractured snout likely caused by ramming into a hard object.
facts.quote: One T. kansasensis specimen possesses two fractured ribs that fully healed. Another T. proriger skull shows a fractured snout, probably caused by ramming into a hard object such as a rock.

facts.statement: Throughout its ~20 million-year history, Tylosaurus was endemic to the North Atlantic Circle Basin, including the North Atlantic, Western Interior Seaway, and Mediterranean Tethys above 30°N.
facts.quote: Throughout its ~20 million-year history, Tylosaurus was endemic to the North Atlantic Circle Basin, a geographic region comprising the North Atlantic and neighboring waters including the Western Interior Seaway in North America and Mediterranean Tethys in Europe above 30°N.

facts.statement: Much of the North Atlantic Circle Basin where Tylosaurus lived was encompassed by a temperate ocean climate.
facts.quote: Much of the region was encompassed by a temperate ocean climate.

facts.statement: The genus Tylosaurus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1872.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1872

facts.statement: Tylosaurus belongs to the subfamily Tylosaurinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Tylosaurinae

facts.statement: The genus Tylosaurus has had the synonyms Rhamphosaurus and Rhinosaurus.
facts.quote: synonyms: * Rhamphosaurus Rhinosaurus

facts.statement: Fossils of Tylosaurus date to the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cretácico Superior

facts.statement: The name Macrosaurus proriger was originally proposed by Cope in 1868 for a fragmentary skull and thirteen vertebrae collected near Monument Rocks in western Kansas.
facts.quote: Originalmente, el nombre "Macrosaurus" proriger fue propuesto por Cope para un cráneo fragmentario y trece vértebras recolectadas cerca de Monument Rocks en el oeste de Kansas en 1868.

facts.statement: Marsh established the name Tylosaurus in 1872 to include original Harvard material and more complete specimens found in Kansas.
facts.quote: Marsh finalmente erigió el nombre Tylosaurus recién en 1872, para incluir el material original de Harvard así como también los especímenes más completos que fueron hallados en Kansas.

facts.statement: A specimen of T. proriger recovered in 1911 by C. D. Bunker near Wallace, Kansas, is one of the largest Tylosaurus skeletons ever found.
facts.quote: Un espécimen de T. proriger, recuperado en 1911 por C. D. Bunker cerca de Wallace, Kansas es uno de los mayores esqueletos de Tylosaurus jamás hallados.

facts.statement: In 1918, Charles H. Sternberg found a Tylosaurus specimen containing the remains of a plesiosaur in its stomach.
facts.quote: En 1918, Charles H. Sternberg halló un Tylosaurus con restos de un plesiosaurio en su estómago.

facts.statement: Information about important Tylosaurus specimens reported by C. H. Sternberg in 1922 was lost to science until 2001.
facts.quote: Aunque estos importantes especímenes fueron reportados brevemente por C. H. Sternberg (1922), la información se perdió para la ciencia hasta 2001.

facts.statement: The Tylosaurus specimen with plesiosaur remains was rediscovered and described by Everhart in 2004.
facts.quote: Este espécimen fue redescubierto y descrito por Everhart (2004a).

facts.statement: A photograph of a Tylosaurus skull was taken by George F. Sternberg around 1926 after he collected and prepared the specimen.
facts.quote: Una fotografía de un cráneo de Tylosaurus fue tomada por George F. Sternberg en torno a 1926 después de que él recolectara y preparara el ejemplar.

facts.statement: The Tylosaurus skull specimen photographed by George F. Sternberg was discovered in the Smoky Hill chalk of Logan County, Kansas.
facts.quote: Éste fue descubierto en la creta de Smoky Hill de Logan County, Kansas.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus is an extinct genus of mosasaurid, named from Greek words meaning "protuberance" and "lizard".
facts.quote: Tylosaurus (del griego τυλος tylos "protuberancia" + σαυρος sauros "lagarto") es un género extinto de mosasáurido

facts.statement: Tylosaurus proriger lived from the late Santonian to mid-Campanian stages in North America, including Kansas, Alabama, and Nebraska.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus proriger (Cope, 1869), del Santoniense tardío hasta mediados del Campaniense de América del Norte (Kansas, Alabama, Nebraska, etc.)

facts.statement: Tylosaurus haumuriensis lived from the early to mid-Campanian stage in New Zealand.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus haumuriensis (Hector, 1874; =Taniwhasaurus oweni), del Campaniano inferior hasta mediados del mismo de Nueva Zelanda

facts.statement: Tylosaurus kansasensis lived during the late Coniacian stage in Kansas.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus kansasensis Everhart, 2005, del Coniaciense tardío de Kansas.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus proriger was among the largest mosasaurs, with the largest specimens reaching lengths of 12.8 to 13.7 meters.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus proriger (y junto con Hainosaurus bernardi y Mosasaurus hoffmannii) estuvo entre los mayores de todos los mosasaurios, los especímenes más grandes que se han encontrado contaban con longitudes de 12.8 a 13.7 metros.

facts.statement: A distinctive feature of Tylosaurus is its elongated and cylindrical premaxilla (snout), from which it takes its name.
facts.quote: Una característica distintiva de Tylosaurus es su alargado y cilíndrico premaxilar (el hocico) del cual toma su nombre

facts.statement: The elongated snout of Tylosaurus may have been used to ram and stun prey, as well as in intraspecific combat.
facts.quote: el cual pudo haber usado para embestir y aturdir a sus presas y también pudo haberlo usado en combates intraespecíficos.

facts.statement: Stomach contents associated with Tylosaurus proriger specimens indicate a varied diet including fish, sharks, smaller mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, and flightless seabirds like Hesperornis.
facts.quote: Contenidos estomacales asociados con especímenes de Tylosaurus proriger indican que este feroz mosasaurio tenía una dieta variada, incluyendo peces, tiburones, mosasaurios menores, plesiosaurios y aves marinas no voladoras como Hesperornis.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus appears to have preferred shallow coastal waters in some environments, such as the Eutaw and Mooreville Chalk formations in Alabama, while favoring deep offshore waters in others, such as the Niobrara chalk in western USA.
facts.quote: En algunos paleoambientes, Tylosaurus parece haber preferido aguas someras, cercanas a las costas (como en la formación Eutaw y la formación Mooreville Chalk de Alabama), mientras favorecía aguas profundas muy alejadas de las costas en otros ambientes (como en la creta de Niobrara del oeste de EE. UU.).

facts.statement: The size, shape, and spacing of the bite marks on the hadrosaur fossil closely resemble the teeth of Tylosaurus proriger.
facts.quote: El tamaño, forma y espacio sin embargo, se parecen mucho a los dientes de Tylosaurus proriger.

facts.statement: The distribution of bite marks on the hadrosaur fossil corresponds inversely to the presence of meat on the animal's body.
facts.quote: La distribución de las marcas de mordida corresponden inversamente a la presencia de carne en el cuerpo del animal.

facts.statement: A Tylosaurus measuring approximately 10 meters in length was found in Kansas by Alan Komrosky in 2009 and is now displayed at the Museum of World Treasures in Wichita, Kansas.
facts.quote: Un Tylosaurus de cerca de 10 metros de largo encontrado en Kansas por Alan Komrosky en 2009 está ahora en exhibición en el Museum of World Treasures en Wichita, Kansas.

facts.statement: Early depictions of Tylosaurus often showed a dorsal crest, but this feature was based on misidentified tracheal cartilage rather than actual anatomy.
facts.quote: Esta y otras imágenes similares estaban basadas en cartílagos traqueales mal identificados, pero cuando el error fue descubierto, ya era una tendencia representar mosasaurios con dichas crestas.

facts.statement: In the documentary "Speckles The Tarbosaurus," two Tylosaurus specimens are shown with exaggerated sizes of over 20 meters each, hunting a Tyrannosaurus, though the latter never lived in Asia.
facts.quote: Dos ejemplares de Tylosaurus aparecen al final del documental "Speckles The Tarbosaurus" (en inglés), ambientado en Mongolia. Éstos depredadores marinos se muestran con una talla exagerada (de más de 20 metros cada uno) y capturando al antagonista, un Tyrannosaurus (el cual jamás habitó en Asia)
